# Prediction Markets Daily
> **Verdx seeks Canadian approval so investors can trade standalone event contracts.**

**What You Need to Know:** Verdx, founded by former finance executives, is seeking approval to enter Canada as an investment dealer for event contracts, under rules that keep sports and elections off the menu. Ark Invest has bought Kalshi shares in three funds, and Cathie Wood praised the company's management. Separately, the CFTC is probing a former lawmaker's Kalshi trades, while MGM and Caesars are staying out over licensing risk.

### Top Story
The Peak, citing the Globe and Mail, reports that Verdx is seeking regulatory approval to enter the Canadian market. Former finance-industry executives founded it, and the platform would be classified as an investment dealer for retail and institutional investors. Unlike the prediction market Wealthsimple launched earlier this year as one offering inside a larger company, Verdx would be a standalone product focused on event contracts. Co-founder Atul Tiwari argued in a Globe and Mail op-ed earlier this year that such platforms would give investors hedging tools and that regulated options would stifle grey-market participation. He compared that case to Ontario's iGaming system, where participation with licensed operators rose from 30 percent to 84 percent over three to four years, The Peak reports. Under Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization rules, operators may offer wagers only on economic indicators, financial markets, and climate trends, not sporting events or political elections. The Peak's QH says that iGaming comparison does not work, because without sports and politics it will be hard to attract Canadians already using VPNs to reach platforms like Kalshi, while institutional investors who must stay aboveboard are the clearer demand. Source: [readthepeak.com](https://www.readthepeak.com/p/canada-could-be-getting-another-prediction-market)

### The Ecosystem
**CFTC probes Kinzinger's Kalshi bets on Biden pardons: Bloomberg**
Bloomberg reported on October 1 that the CFTC is probing former lawmaker Kinzinger's Kalshi bets on Biden pardons, which is an investigation, not a published finding or a judgment. Source: [bloomberg.com](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-01/cftc-probes-ex-lawmaker-kinzinger-s-kalshi-bets-on-biden-pardons)

**Cathie Wood praises Kalshi as Ark discloses a private-share stake: Benzinga**
Benzinga reports that Ark Invest chief executive Cathie Wood said on X, "Kalshi's management team is phenomenal, as it is skating to where the prediction markets puck will be." Those comments followed Ark's September 18 purchase of Kalshi shares, bought directly from private markets, across three actively managed ETFs. The ARK Innovation ETF picked up 90,024 shares, the ARK Next Generation Internet ETF added 25,318, and the ARK Fintech Innovation ETF bought 11,252, a combined 126,594 shares. Ark estimates the medium-term prediction-market opportunity at 1 trillion to 5 trillion dollars in annual notional volume, according to its analyst Nick Grous. Benzinga states that Kalshi currently handles more than 90 percent of U.S. activity. Ark flagged state-level legal challenges, competition from Robinhood, and potential pressure on take rates, and said it believes the upside outweighs them. Source: [benzinga.com](https://www.benzinga.com/etfs/specialty-etfs/26/10/62128505/cathie-wood-calls-kalshi-leadership-phenomenal-ark-invest-stake)

**MGM and Caesars decline prediction markets over licensing risk: Gambling News**
Gambling News reports on October 2 that MGM and Caesars say no to prediction markets over licensing risks. Source: [gamblingnews.com](https://www.gamblingnews.com/news/mgm-and-caesars-say-no-to-prediction-markets-over-licensing-risks/)

NPR reports that a man banned by betting sites, who had filed for bankruptcy, then relapsed on Kalshi. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/02/nx-s1-5981420/kalshi-betting-prediction-markets-gambling-addiction)

**New York gambling-tax revenue tops $1 billion: Business Insider**
Business Insider reports on October 2 that New York gets over 1 billion dollars in revenue from taxes on gambling, and that prediction markets could shake that up. Source: [businessinsider.com](https://www.businessinsider.com/new-york-gambling-tax-revenue-faces-loss-prediction-market-growth-2026-10)

### The Board
Will the U.S. invade Iran before 2027? Yes is priced at a 14.5 percent implied probability on Polymarket, with 555,000 dollars in 24-hour volume, read at 2026-10-02 11:20 UTC.
Is Donut Battery essentially lithium free? Yes is priced at a 19.8 percent implied probability on Manifold, play money, with 6,265 mana in 24-hour volume and 179 traders, read at 2026-10-02 11:20 UTC.
Access to these venues, and to which contracts, depends on where the listener lives, and those rules are changing. Source: [polymarket.com](https://polymarket.com/event/will-the-us-invade-iran-before-2027) Source: [manifold.markets](https://manifold.markets/MikhailTal/donut-battery-is-essentially-lithiu)

### New and Notable
No contract in today's material opened in the last three days, and no article reports a newly listed market.

### How It Works: How Markets Aggregate Information
A market price pools scattered information when the trade is the message. Someone holding a private signal buys or sells, the quote moves, and the next person meets a number that already contains that signal. An automated market maker can post the quote without a human taking the other side.

Information Aggregation in Exponential Family Markets, a 2014 paper on arXiv, shows those makers can be designed from exponential family distributions, a standard template in statistics. It connects price aggregation to the way learning agents pool beliefs when they use the same distributions. Under exponential utility, a form of risk aversion, the paper analyzes market behavior and the price equilibrium. It also considers traders who face a budget constraint rather than that utility alone.

Final prices are a weaker record than they look. Are Final Market Prices Sufficient for Information Aggregation?, a 2025 paper on arXiv, studies parimutuel betting on horse races, where a wager cannot be made contingent on the final odds. Interim odds show expected returns depend on the path, not only the finish: horses whose odds declined in the final five minutes earned higher realized returns than horses with similar final odds. A two-period extension of the Ottaviani and Sørensen information model accounts for the pattern, with late declines coming from informed bettors wagering on private signals. The paper adds that final-odds and return patterns alone may not separate information aggregation from probability distortions.

A reader cannot treat the last price as a complete file of what was known. The path into the price matters, and so does whether anyone could contract on the price that eventually printed. The racing measurement describes those markets. It is not a method for any contract.

# Prediction Markets Daily
> **Two White House reviews leave event-contract rules unbinding for traders and states.**

**What You Need to Know:** Two White House reviews of CFTC event-contract actions have not produced operative rules. As of October 1, a proposed rule that would fold event contracts into the swap definition and an interim final rule that would exclude casino-style products were still unpublished. A September 25 Sixth Circuit decision already allowed Ohio and Tennessee to treat the sports contracts in that case under state gambling law.

### Top Story
As of October 1, neither CFTC event-contract submission that reached White House review on September 28 was a published, operative rule, Crypto News reports. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs lists RIN 3038-AF82 as a proposed rule that would define a swap to include event contracts, and RIN 3038-AF81 as an interim final rule that would exclude casino-style gambling products; the complete text was not in the Federal Register. Receipt by the review office does not make either measure binding, and review can still change the wording, the timing, or whether a measure is issued. On September 25 the Sixth Circuit held that the sports contracts before it were not swaps and allowed Ohio and Tennessee to apply state gambling laws. The account cites CFTC data that designated markets certified about 1,600 new event contracts in 2025, against roughly five a year from 2006 through 2020. Source: [crypto.news](https://crypto.news/the-cftc-has-sent-prediction-market-rules-to-the-white-house-states-are-still-in-court/)

The first-round contract has Lula at about 67 to 71 percent implied probability, and the price of any candidate winning that round outright is about 6 percent. The first round is scheduled for October 4, 2026. Those figures are contract prices, not bookmaker quotes, and they can move with trading flow as well as with expectations. Source: [99bitcoins.com](https://99bitcoins.com/news/presales/brazil-election-polymarket-odds/)

### New and Notable
Polymarket has listed a new contract on when the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 will form. The listing says the season had no hurricanes as of October 1 and only eight weak tropical storms, that the National Hurricane Center expected no formation in the next seven days, and that. is part of that listing's stated backdrop. Source: [polymarket.com](https://polymarket.com/event/when-will-the-first-hurricane-form-in-the-atlantic-in-2026-20260930143512296)

### How It Works: Arbitrage: When Two Venues Disagree
A winner-take-all set is built to be exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so related prices should add to one dollar. Falling short of that dollar, or running past it, is a bound that follows from the payoff at settlement. It is not automatically a position a trader can close while the market is still open.

A 2025 arXiv paper on Polymarket names two forms of that gap. Market-rebalancing arbitrage sits inside one market. Combinatorial arbitrage runs across related markets. From on-chain order-book history, the authors estimate about 40 million dollars of profit extracted. A full comparison of every linked condition does not scale, so they narrowed the search by timing, topic, and combinatorial relationship.

A 2026 arXiv paper splits the bound again. Payoff-space no-arbitrage follows from terminal payoffs. Protocol-executable no-arbitrage depends on the conversions a trader can actually make before settlement. On Polymarket's negative-risk markets, linked binaries stand for mutually exclusive outcomes, but the NegRisk Adapter operationalizes only the NO-to-YES direction before settlement. Reconstructing depth-aware portfolios and on-chain conversion traces, the authors estimate 1.12 million dollars of arbitrage profit: 1.086 million from converter-enabled strategies and 32 thousand from baskets held to settlement. In the order-book sample, positive violations concentrated on the unsupported YES side, while adapter-supported NO-side violations were less frequent and shorter-lived. The authors' reading is that a pre-settlement conversion strengthens enforcement by reducing capital lock-up and letting inventory recycle. They also built a prototype that would make the reverse path executable before settlement.

When two prices disagree, the same constraint applies. A gap is enforceable only if a trader can turn one position into the other before resolution. Where that conversion is missing, the bound can sit until the contract pays.

# Prediction Markets Daily
> **A dozen jobs against 1.8 million is the casino lobby's case against prediction markets.**

**What You Need to Know:** The American Gaming Association says it is on a "war-time footing" over prediction markets in the United States. President Bill Miller made that case at the G2E conference in Las Vegas, and the chief executives of MGM, Caesars and Wynn said the markets should be state-licensed. The fight he described is about state gambling law, tribal sovereignty, taxes and who may buy an event contract.

### Top Story
At the G2E conference in Las Vegas, American Gaming Association president Bill Miller said the U.S. casino trade group is on a "war-time footing" over the rise of prediction markets. He said the markets are "trying to prop themselves up," ignore state laws, tax systems and tribal casino sovereignty, and that regulated operators "come in through the front door" while "well-funded bad guys" have "kicked in the back door." The CEOs of MGM, Caesars and Wynn, whom TheLines.com described as Nevada's largest gambling operators, backed him and said prediction markets should be state-licensed. Miller said regulated U.S. gaming "supports 1.8 million [American] jobs," against "maybe a dozen jobs" from what he called the "cashmere hoodie bros in Brooklyn." TheLines.com reported his further case that the markets stretch the Commodity Exchange Act past its original intent, frame gambling as investing, and can be bought at 18 because they are regulated federally as derivatives, against 21 at many U.S. online betting sites. Source: [thelines.com](https://www.thelines.com/prediction-markets/industry-news/american-gaming-association-on-war-time-footing-over-prediction-markets/)

### How It Works: The Law: Event Contracts, Regulators and the Courts
An event contract is a promise with a price. The buyer pays now. If the stated event happens, the contract pays a fixed sum. If it does not, the contract pays nothing. In the United States, that shape is what pulls the instrument toward the Commodity Exchange Act and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. State authorities have treated the same instrument as gambling. Which label wins is not settled.

A 2026 Note in the Boston College Law Review says political prediction markets have existed in limited formats since 1988 and returned to public view in the 2024 elections, when platforms such as Kalshi offered trades on United States presidential and congressional races. The Note asks whether those trades are legal. It records that the CFTC said no and a federal district court said yes. Examining the statutory source of the agency's power to review trades based on the outcome of events, sometimes called event contracts, the Note concludes that the law is contradictory and unclear. It also concludes that political prediction markets benefit the public, and it recommends new Commodity Exchange Act language that would narrow the CFTC's authority to review event contracts and clarify the public-interest standard used in that review. That recommendation is the Note's. It is not an enacted amendment.

The same definitional problem appears under other statutes. A 2015 article in the Victoria University of Wellington Law Review examines New Zealand's Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013, which it calls the most substantial overhaul of that country's securities law in recent history, and asks how the Act treats the prediction market iPredict. Its conclusion is narrow: iPredict can operate under the Act only if the Financial Markets Authority declares that its contracts are derivatives and grants substantial exemptions from regulatory compliance. The author then recommends a more coherent approach by analogy with the Act's prescribed intermediary service licences.

For someone reading a market, the label decides the pipe the contract travels through: who may list it, who may be shut out, and which public-interest test a regulator applies. The Boston College Note's finding is that, on political event contracts in the United States, that test still sits in contradictory statute. What is unsettled should be read as unsettled.

### New and Notable

### How It Works: Who Decides the Answer? Resolution, Rules and Oracles
A crypto-settled contract does not pay when traders converge. Collateral stays locked until an oracle delivers a result and winning claims can be redeemed. That handoff is the oracle problem, as an ACM Computing Surveys paper frames it: a smart contract can read on-chain data, but the event the question is about lives off-chain, so some mechanism has to move the outside result onto the chain.

The survey splits oracle implementations into two groups. Voting-based designs finalize an outcome mainly from participants' stakes. Reputation-based designs combine reputation and performance metrics with authenticity-proof mechanisms aimed at data correctness and integrity. Both are described as ways to give a smart contract final feedback. The paper closes by noting remaining challenges and future research directions, without treating either family as settled.

A separate arXiv paper measures what the wait does to the price. When collateral remains locked until oracle settlement, a near-certain dollar is a delayed dollar, so the price embeds a maturity-dependent settlement discount in addition to beliefs about the outcome. The authors recover an implied settlement-discount term structure from persistent near-certain contracts, using realized settlement times, and summarize it as an annualized settlement wedge. The recovered wedges are positive, maturity-dependent, and time-varying. Adjusting prices by those curves reduces the near-certainty horizon gradient by roughly 48 to 88 percent, which the paper treats as evidence that much of the raw maturity pattern is priced settlement friction rather than forecast error alone.

Design changes the wedge. negRisk conversion compresses discounts by recycling part of the position into synthetic collateral. Yield-bearing collateral flattens the term structure by reducing the opportunity cost of lock-up. On this account, pricing quality is endogenous to settlement mechanics, collateral productivity, and capital-recycling design. A price near certainty is a belief plus a claim on money that cannot move until the named resolution process — an oracle report, a stake-weighted vote, or a reputation-weighted check — says the question is closed.

# Prediction Markets Daily
> **Two million dollars from Kalshi has Nevada and Michigan pulling support from the national problem-gambling council.**

**What You Need to Know:** The National Council on Problem Gambling may look for a new director after a Kalshi research gift, and regulators in Nevada and Michigan have already withdrawn support. Product and policy notes today cover stock-linked contracts, a tax plea to the IRS, a limit on Polymarket identity checks, and margin clearance for Kalshi professional clients. Two Polymarket contracts supply the priced reads.

### Top Story
The same account says the possible search may be tied to controversy over a Kalshi donation, but not necessarily. After the council accepted $2 million from Kalshi, gaming regulators in Nevada and Michigan withdrew their support. The council says it is focused on harm wherever it occurs, prediction markets included, that it will not take up whether the products are legal, and that the money is to advance understanding of how prediction markets inflict harm. Former director of programs Jaime Costello resigned and, on LinkedIn, moved to dispel rumors that the resignation was related to the Kalshi donation.

### The Ecosystem
**Prediction markets' push into US stocks raises regulatory alarm bells:** Reuters
A push by prediction markets into U.S. stocks is raising regulatory alarm bells, Reuters reports. Source: [reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/prediction-markets-push-into-us-stocks-raises-regulatory-alarm-bells-2026-09-28/)

**Professors Urge IRS to Clear Up Prediction Market Tax Confusion:** Gambling Insider
Professors are urging the Internal Revenue Service to clear up confusion over the tax treatment of prediction markets, Gambling Insider reports. Source: [gamblinginsider.com](https://www.gamblinginsider.com/news/196133/irs-prediction-market-tax-rules)

**Polymarket Says KYC Applies Only to New Beta Product, Not Existing Platform:** CoinMarketCap
Polymarket says know-your-customer checks apply only to a new beta product, not to the existing platform, CoinMarketCap reports. Source: [coinmarketcap.com](https://coinmarketcap.com/academy/article/polymarket-kyc-beta-product)

**Kalshi Gets Margin Trading Clearance for Professional Clients:** CoinMarketCap

### How It Works: Can a Prediction Market Be Manipulated?
A contract can settle on a number its own holders are free to trade. That is settlement manipulation in plain form. A paper posted to arXiv on June 30, 2026, models contracts that pay on an asset price holders can move by trading the underlying. The model says those contracts transfer wealth from prediction-market liquidity traders to manipulators. It also says they harm price discovery in the underlying, even as that market becomes more liquid. After Polymarket launched a five-minute Bitcoin contract, settlement-time spot order flow spiked. The spikes caused large price reversals after settlement. Manipulators captured a large amount of profit, mostly from retail. Manipulation was largely absent in the fifteen-minute contracts. Lengthening the horizon removed it, and the authors call that the market-design remedy their model and evidence support.

A second paper, posted to arXiv on January 28, 2026, pairs agent-based simulation with an analytic account of price dynamics. Bettors differ in expertise, noisy private information, learning rates and budgets, and they watch public opinion on the outcome before they bet. The simulated market is stable across a broad parameter space. Complex behavior and price interactions produce self-regulatory price discovery. A highly resourced minority — a whale — with a biased valuation can still shift the price, and the shift is temporary. The move is larger and lasts longer when other bettors herd and learn slowly. Theory in the paper says whales shift prices in proportion to their share of market capital. How long the distortion lasts depends on non-whale learning rates and on how intensely those bettors herd.

A short contract on a tradable price is the case where the defense fails in this evidence. A longer horizon is the fix that paper measured. A binary book can be shoved by capital share and herding, then pull back if the rest of the book keeps learning.

### New and Notable

### How It Works: Markets Against Polls
In a continuous double auction, traders buy and sell contracts and can be ranked by what they earn. A prediction poll, in the test that follows, asks each person for a probability instead, alone or in a team, and ranks those judgments with a Brier score.

Management Science published that head-to-head test in 2017. The paper reports the first large-scale, long-term experimental comparison of the two methods. More than 2,400 people forecast 261 events across two seasons of a geopolitical prediction tournament, and they were randomly assigned to markets or to polls. Uri Gneezy accepted the paper for the journal’s behavioral economics area.

Market prices were more accurate than the simple average of poll forecasts in both seasons. Team polls then beat the markets, but only after the forecasts were combined with temporal decay, more weight for forecasters who had done well before, and recalibration. The polls’ largest edge appeared at the start of questions that still had a long time to run.

That pattern is the useful limit. A raw average of probability judgments lost to the market price. A statistically aggregated team poll did not. The gap favored the polls earliest, on the longest questions. Proper scoring feedback and collaboration were part of the poll design that produced the stronger aggregated result. A price is one way to compress a crowd. It is not the only way, and in this tournament it was not always the most accurate way. None of these comparisons is a suggestion to take either side of a contract.

### How It Works: The Favourite-Longshot Bias
In a parimutuel market, the favorite-longshot bias is a return pattern: the expected return on an outcome tends to rise with the share of bets placed on that outcome. A 2010 paper in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics treats that pattern as something to test, not as a fixed law. It ties the direction and the size of the bias to the ratio of private information to noise in the market. That ratio, the paper says, should show up in observables: how many people are betting, how many outcomes are on offer, how much private information is around, how much participation comes from recreational interest, whether bets can be divided finely, whether noise arrives after the fact, and whether outcomes were already unequal before anyone bet.

A September 2026 paper looks for the same pattern on Polymarket, using 588 million trades by 2.48 million accounts. In the trades as they happened, purchases below 10 cents lost 19.3 cents per dollar. Purchases at or above 90 cents earned 0.83 cents per dollar. Grouping changes the picture. When each contract is weighted equally, longshots lost 6.3 cents per dollar. When related contracts are first grouped by parent event, those longshots gained 4.1 cents per dollar. The two-sided pattern — cheap contracts losing, expensive ones gaining a little — held in crypto and politics and was absent in sports. Accounts with the strongest past habit of buying longshots, the top tenth, made 26.6 percent of the next month's low-price purchases and earned returns similar to everyone else. The top tenth of accounts that had been buying favorites made 15.1 percent of the next month's high-price purchases and earned less than others. The paper's claim is an aggregate favorite-longshot bias on Polymarket whose size depends on how contracts are grouped. A price near zero or near one is not, on this evidence, a clean read of probability; the grouping of the contract, and whether the market is sports, politics, or crypto, changes the return that price has delivered. Those figures describe past trades. They are not a reason to take either side of any contract.

### How It Works: Calibration: What It Means for a Forecast to Be Right
Calibration means the stated probability matches how often the outcome arrives, across many events rather than one. A sixty percent forecast is calibrated, in that class of calls, if the event happens about sixty percent of the time. Sharpness is separate: probability mass near zero or one, rather than near fifty percent. Sharp and calibrated are not the same thing. One surprising result does not make the forecast wrong, because the score is taken over the set, after the events resolve.

Monthly Weather Review in 2013 describes an improvement to ensemble kernel density model output statistics, called EKDMOS. Model output statistics equations are multiple linear regressions relating observations to ensemble-mean predictors. Spread-skill relationships are one-term linear regressions that predict the ensemble mean’s expected accuracy from the ensemble spread. The method applies the equations to each member, fits a probability density by kernel density fitting, and adjusts that density’s spread to the spread predicted by the spread-skill relationship. On North American Ensemble Forecast System two-meter temperature forecasts from October 1, 2007, through March 31, 2010, the improved EKDMOS forecasts were more reliable than an earlier spread adjustment and than rank-sorting bias-corrected members, with a better calibrated spread-error relationship and more day-to-day spread variability.

Weather and Forecasting in 2010 compares bias correction with spatial disaggregation and an analog method on daily precipitation forecasts from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts Ensemble Prediction System, over a ten-day period, for the Ohio River basin from 2002 through 2006, against Tropical Rainfall Monitoring Mission observations. Neither beat a simple spatial-interpolation benchmark on forecast skill. Both improved reliability, the analog more so. Bias correction improved the bias for all forecast amounts, less so for large amounts, but the downscaled patterns were unrealistic. The analog reduced biases over a wider range of amounts and produced more realistic patterns.

Reading a market, reliability is whether the price’s implied probability matches later frequency, and sharpness is how far that price sits from fifty percent. Those tests show a fix can improve reliability without improving skill against a simple benchmark. A single resolution does not settle calibration, including when a market is thin or the stake is play money.

### How It Works: Liquidity, Spreads and Thin Markets
Automated market makers in prediction markets recruit third-party liquidity providers who deposit assets and earn fees from trades. The arXiv paper Bootstrapping Liquidity in BTC-Denominated Prediction Markets shows cross-market making against stablecoin venues supplies the most user-friendly risk profile yet requires active professional makers or platform subsidies. The same paper finds DeFi redirection of user trades enables rapid bootstrapping but exposes participants to liquidation thresholds and exchange-rate volatility. A General Theory of Liquidity Provisioning for Prediction Markets demonstrates that protocols allowing arbitrary cost functions can run multiple market makers in parallel while recovering existing DeFi approaches as special cases. Liquidity expressed as a matrix-valued function becomes necessary once three or more securities trade because single-dimensional parameters cannot cover the full price space. Thin markets move sharply on single trades because limited depth leaves wide bid-ask spreads that one order can cross. Listeners can identify thin markets by low 24-hour volume relative to open interest and by observing large price jumps after modest trading activity. The papers note that automated market making remains simple to deploy but carries capital inefficiency and permanent loss risk for providers. Cross-market making trades stability for the need for ongoing professional oversight.

# Prediction Markets Daily
> **CFTC staff say mention markets may be presumed open to manipulation.**

**What You Need to Know:** Staff at the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission told designated contract markets on September 22 that contracts settling on what a named person says, attends or does may be presumed readily susceptible to manipulation. The advisory does not ban those contracts and does not create new legal obligations; it asks exchanges for a heightened showing before listing them. Kalshi is seeking approval for margin on event contracts, Missouri’s attorney general has sent cease-and-desist letters to six operators, and Yahoo Finance has ended a Polymarket deal.

### What This Show Covers
A prediction market lets people trade on whether something will happen. A contract is written around a question and a resolution rule, and the price traders will pay can be read as the crowd’s probability that the answer is yes. That reading is the idea under examination here: when a price works as a forecast, and when the design of the market, the rules, or the people who can move the outcome make it a poor one.

Each episode has the same shape. The regulators, courts and lawmakers deciding what these markets may be come first — the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, state attorneys general and gaming authorities, and regulators outside the United States — and a legal story names the jurisdiction it is actually about. Then the venues, the products and the people building or contesting them. A short board lists a handful of the day’s most traded questions, each with its venue, its volume and the time the price was read, so a probability is never a free-floating number. One explainer walks through how a piece of the machinery works.

This show will not tell anyone what to trade. It reports and explains. It does not recommend buying, selling or holding a contract, and it does not offer a pick, a tip or a view on which side is mispriced. The law is not one rule. It differs by country, province and state, and it is changing; when a story is about the law, the show says whose rules, and it states a specific legal fact only when a dated source supports it.

Prediction Markets Daily is part of the Nerra Network, an independent, ad-free network of shows at nerranetwork.com. Listeners who want the rest of the network can find it there.

### Top Story
Staff in the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Division of Market Oversight issued an advisory on September 22, 2026, covering contracts that settle on specific words or phrases, event attendance, public appearances and interactions between individuals. The guidance, aimed at designated contract markets, says these mention markets can be presumed readily susceptible to manipulation because settlement can depend on conduct controlled by one named person or a small group, unlike contracts on election results, economic releases or regulated sports. It does not ban the contracts and, unlike a Commission rule, creates no new legal obligations; exchanges remain under the Commodity Exchange Act’s Core Principle 3, which requires them to list only derivatives that are not readily susceptible to manipulation, and staff want a heightened showing, with surveillance built around the people who control the outcome. On August 28 the agency ordered former White House teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez to pay $172,539.02 — $107,539.02 in disgorgement and a $65,000 civil penalty — and imposed a three-year trading ban, after finding he used advance access to presidential speeches to trade mention contracts on Kalshi between December 2025 and February 2026. A month before that order, the agency settled with former Representative George Santos over trading in a Kalshi contract on whether he would attend the State of the Union; he paid $35,000 and did not admit wrongdoing. Kalshi said its internal surveillance flagged the Perez trades and that it reported them to federal authorities. ### How It Works: Why a Price Can Be Read as a Probability
A contract that pays a fixed sum if an event happens, and nothing if it does not, trades at a price between those two payoffs. Buyers are taking the view that the event is more likely than that price; sellers, that it is less likely. Where both sides can trade, the price is where that disagreement has cleared for the moment, which is why it can be read as a probability — the terms on which the market last found a counterparty, not a verdict issued by the venue.

A paper in Management Science compared that reading with another way of pooling forecasts. More than 2,400 participants forecast 261 events over two seasons of a geopolitical tournament. They were randomly assigned to prediction markets — continuous double auctions, ranked on earnings — or to prediction polls, submitting probabilities alone or in teams and ranked on Brier scores. In both seasons, market prices were more accurate than the simple mean of the poll forecasts. Team polls outperformed the markets once forecasts were aggregated using temporal decay, weights based on past performance, and recalibration. The polls’ biggest advantage was at the beginning of long-duration questions.

A paper on cost-function market makers notes that trading in a duality-based design collectively implements Follow-The-Regularized-Leader. Modifying that pricing rule, the authors propose a Smooth Quadratic Prediction Market so that trading implements general steepest gradient descent, with a better worst-case monetary loss for AD securities and with no-arbitrage and an instantaneous price preserved. They also look at bounded budgets and buy-only securities, cases where a clean probability reading leaves something out.

The same research flags a limit: independent judgments, properly aggregated, beat market prices at the start of long questions. This show will not say which contract to buy or sell. Every probability here carries its venue, its volume and the time it was read.
